Stealing from the dead

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate a property developer accused of reneging on life rights contracts signed with the elderly, leaving bereaved family members to accuse them of stealing from the dead.

Unique Selling Point:
Family members of lessees in the Belvedere Retirement Village Group (14 villages with 160 units each, all on the JHB West Rand) are complaining that they are not receiving the money they are owed when their relations pass away and no longer reside in the villages.

Summary:
The group offer life rights deals to the elderly - you pay a sum to the developer and have the right to live in your unit until you either decide to sell it or pass away. You never own the property/unit. If you decide to sell, or if you pass away and the unit is sold, the money should go into a trust. You / or your nominated loved ones, are supposed to receive the full amount you paid for the unit back, while the developer is entitled to any profits made from the sale. BUT THIS IS NOT HAPPENING.

Case Studies:
Lianne Silver: Her mother passed away in Feb 2020. The unit, nr 53 Harveston Estate, cost her R700 000 when she bought it. Lianne and family members were supposed to receive the R700 000 back within 30 days once the unit was sold. It was sold for R1.4 Million in April 2020. But Lianne still has not seen a scent. She has opened both a criminal and civil case against the Belvedere Group and developer Billy E Steyn, who is in charge of the group.

Gavin den Heyer: Has actually won a court case against the group, where the court ordered that Belvedere Group pay out the money owed to den Heyer in monthly instalments. Belvedere are still not paying.

Lyn Cunningham: Her mother gave up her unit in Harveston to be sold, to pay for the costs of frail care she now needs. Although the un it was sold in 2019, Lyn and her mother have still not received any money.

Further information:
Lianne Silver's lawyer, Reon Marais, has agreed to do an on camera interview. He is helping Lianne do the civil and criminal cases. Says that the group have no leg to stand on, contractually they have to pay. Even if their were a longer period involved, to get admin etc sorted, the group cannot not pay after months of already having the been paid for the properties. Also says Belvedere are not using any legal loopholes not to pay, they are simply not paying.

Bill E Steyn is according to a source, returning from his holiday home in George tomorrow, Thursday 28 January. He seems near impossible to get hold of, no one has email address, phone nrs etc for him. The group have two offices, one inside one of the estates, and another which seems to be the address of a law firm in Honeydew. I will start with a written offer of an on camera right of reply to his attorney and and a sales agent if they won't give me his contact details. Should it be necessary to do a confront, we could try door stopping the offices.

Script:


Stealing from the dead
1st Draft Script
03 February 2021

Voice
This is the Harveston Retirement Village, one of 12 similar retirement estates built by brothers and property developers Willem and Billy Steyn. The estates are collectively marketed under the Belvedere Retirement Villages brand. None of the residents here own the units they occupy, instead they’ve all signed life rights agreements with the Belvedere group.

Link
With a life right’s agreement you never own the property, you have the use of it until you pass on, or move on, possibly to a frail care facility. And to many elderly people, it seemed like a golden opportunity.

Voice
Especially since residents are supposed to get the full amount they paid for their life rights back once the unit has been sold by the Belvedere group. According to the agreements, the developers in turn are entitled to any profits they make off the sales. Lianne Silver’s mother, Shirley, was one of the residents at Harveston.

Sound Up Lianne
Derek: Lianne, tell us about your mom?

Lianne: She was quite a dynamic little old lady. She did a lot of things in her life, she worked hard, but family and being there for everyone, that’s what she was. She was there for everyone.

Voice
Sadly her mother, who had been ill for sometime, passed away in February last year from kidney failure.

Sound Up Lianne
It just all happened so suddenly, suddenly she just quickly, within 24 hours, she passed. The kidney just failed, the liver failed, and the doctor said there was no hope of her recovering.

Voice
Shirley had paid paid R777 000 for her life rights in Harveston, and after some deductions due to the developers, Silver says her estate was supposed to receive just over R700 000 from the sale.

Sound Up Lianne
It was meant to be that I wouldn’t have to wait, when she had died, they would have incentive to sell the property, and it all looked so wonderful in the package. And in the contract itself it said 30 days you would be paid out, so it sounded wonderful and rosy.

Voice
The exact wording from the contract says: “Payment will be made only after 30 days from the date that the new occupant has paid the new loan amount to the developer in full.” But although the unit was sold in July of 2020, Silver says they’ve never received the money they’re owed.

Sound Up Lianne
And I’ve tried to phone them, and I’ve tried to confirm dates with them, I get the brush off from them. They’ll ask, they’ll find out.




Voice
In desperation, she turned to lawyer Reon Marais, who her mother had appointed as the executor in her estate. After he made several enquiries about when the payment could be expected, he received this emailed response from the Belvedere group’s attorney on the 5th of November last year.

Sound Up Reon Marais
“Good day, on behalf of the developer we sincerely apologise for the delay in finalising this matter. The repayment of the loan amount was due on the 25th of September 2020.” So on their own version they are saying we should have paid you at that date.

Voice
Nearly a year after her mother passed away, the money is still outstanding. Silver says a portion of it is meant to go to her adopted niece and nephew.

Sound Up Lianne
Lianne: But mostly for my adopted niece and nephew, Kayla and Joshua. So she was most concerned that they would get some money, and that they would have an education. They have stolen her whole life’s work. It’s a disgrace, it really is a disgrace.

Voice
Mike Cunninham’s mother Bernice also had a life rights agreement in the Harveston Retirement Village. By the end of 2019, she could no longer take care of herself, and moved into frail care. As agreed, the Belvedere group put her unit up for sale.

Sound Up Mike Cunningham
Derek: Now has her unit at Harveston been sold?

Mike: Yes it has been sold, people actually took occupation in July of 2020.

Voice
But Cunningham says his mother has not seen the R1,25 million she’s owed from the sale.

Sound Up Mike
And they paid R1,75 million for the place. And I’ve got that documentation in front of me.

Voice
The Steyn brothers agreed to an interview with us, and we met them at the Jacaranda Retirement village, which they also own. Present were members of the different bodies corporate from the retirement villages, as well as their own camera crew. Willem Steyn said the Belvedere group consisted of 12 retirement villages, each owned by a trust.

Sound Up Willem Steyn
Derek: you are on the list of trustees for virtually every unit?

Willem: I am basically on I would say on half, at least the half of them, and Billy is probably on the other half, more or less.

Voice
Both brothers are trustees of the Harveston Aftree Oord Trust, which owns the Harveston Village.

Sound Up Willem

Derek: According to your contracts, you say you will pay people out within 30 days of their units being sold and paid for by the new owners?

Willem: According to our contract we said that we will pay after 30 days, so you must just make sure that the nuances is right.

Voice
But that’s not always how it’s explained to potential buyers. This voice recording of a phone call to one of Belvedere’s sales agents was made earlier this week.

Sound Up Willem Steyn
Sound Phone call: Agent: After it’s sold, when the money comes in, one calendar month after that you get paid out.

Derek: You heard it, one calendar month afterwards you’ll be paid out, being told to a possible client this week. It’s not what you’re telling me now?

Willem: Ja but that’s our intention Derek, and we really strive to do that. We are currently in different times, economically.

Derek: But because we are in difficult times, agents shouldn’t be making those promises?

Willem: I will in that case speak to my agents.

Voice
The Steyn’s don’t deny owing the money to Lianne Silver or Bernice Cunningham.


Sound Up Willem
Willem: You are absolutely right Derek, they should have been paid, but they are not yet paid, but they will be paid.

Voice
Despite the Steyn’s having been paid in both cases, and made profit off the sales, they say the Covid 19 pandemic has put a severe strain on their cash flow.

Sound Up Billy Steyn
As Willem also explained, we are still struggling to get funds in, in terms of normal operation, from last year with Covid, lockdowns with council, lockdowns with the deeds office etc.

Voice
But for brothers Gavin and Darryl den Heyer, that’s not a valid excuse. They say they’ve been struggling to get their mother Sheila’s payment out of the Belvedere group since she passed away in 2017, many years before the Covid pandemic hit South Africa.

Sound Up Darryl den Heyer
The contract was very clear, and we had to wait 30 days after the money was in, and then we would be paid out. And that came, and it went, and we carried on. I sent mails, tried to get hold of them, and we just had no luck. Nothing came back to us.

Voice
After a year of trying, the brothers approached Schindlers Attorney’s. Associate Andrew Lawrie is acting on their behalf. He approached the court for a summary judgement against the Harveston trust.

Sound Up Andrew Lawrie
If you have good grounds to believe the defendant has no real defence, and that they are just trying to buy time, you can go for summary judgement.

Voice
The trust offered to settle the matter before the case appeared in court. According to the settlement, the trust would pay out the sum of R1 115 000 in five instalments between August and December of 2019.

Sound Up Andrew
The settlement agreement was made an order of court mind you, so this was not just an agreement between two people, this was a court stamped document, a court order.

Voice
But despite a high court order, no payments have been forthcoming.

Sound Up Willem
Derek: This goes back four years, way before Covid.

Willem: That is probably so, but they chose to litigate. And the problem is with litigation…

Derek: But only out of frustration Willem

Willem: Ja, well

Derek: But why this case, why didn’t you pay them? Is there a reason?

Willem: Ok let’s go back, let’s take a snapshot, and thats what we are doing here today, we’re talking about 2, 3, 4, 20 people right now that’s not been paid? So…

Derek: But that’s 20 too many Willem, that’s 20 families waiting to be paid out, or elderly people waiting to pay for frail care.

Willem: That is two percent of the business.

Voice
A business that seems well protected by it’s cleverly structured trusts.

Sound Up Willem
Derek: Willem it is alleged that you are using this complex network of trusts to provide you with legal protection, and to make it costly and difficult for anyone who’s owed money to take you to court?

Willem: Correct Derek.

Voice
He says the retirement villages are worth billions, and he needs to protect his assets.

Sound Up Willem
More than R2 billion if I look at that. There is no ways that anybody will open themselves to any creditor or anybody coming from the outside.

Derek: R2 Billion?

Willem: On the retirement villages yes. And the question is you are going to ask me why don’t I pay people back? There’s a difference between assets and cash flow.

Derek: And everybody is going to say Willem is stinking rich he could pay these people today?

Willem: Exactly.

Derek: Is that true?

Willem: So I hope to do it as soon as I can…

Derek: So you are stinking rich?

Willem: I’m not rich, I’m wealthy.

Derek: Wealthy, ok.

Willem: Stinking wealthy.

Voice
The den Heyers, Mike Cunningham and Lianne Silver are all taking further legal action, but it’s been a bitter pill to swallow for family members not lucky enough to be sitting on assets worth billions of rands.

Sound Up Lianne
My sister’s children need this money. It’s not as if they are millionaires, they are not. They need this money






Promos

Promo 1
Distraught family members, and property assets worth billions, we investigate retirement village developers who stand accused of breaking their promises to the vulnerable and elderly.

Promo 2
Their contracts said when their life rights units were sold, they’d be paid within a month. Or so they thought. We investigate property developers accused of reneging on promises to the elderly.

Promo 3
We investigate a property group worth billions after selling life rights deals to the elderly. Why are some family members having to fight for years in court to get their loved ones money back.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate a property developer accused of reneging on life rights contracts signed with the elderly, leaving bereaved family members to accuse them of stealing from the dead.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Family members of lessees in the Belvedere Retirement Village Group (14 villages with 160 units each, all on the JHB West Rand) are complaining that they are not receiving the money they are owed when their relations pass away and no longer reside in the villages.
metadata.Summary: The group offer life rights deals to the elderly - you pay a sum to the developer and have the right to live in your unit until you either decide to sell it or pass away. You never own the property/unit. If you decide to sell, or if you pass away and the unit is sold, the money should go into a trust. You / or your nominated loved ones, are supposed to receive the full amount you paid for the unit back, while the developer is entitled to any profits made from the sale. BUT THIS IS NOT HAPPENING. Case Studies: Lianne Silver: Her mother passed away in Feb 2020. The unit, nr 53 Harveston Estate, cost her R700 000 when she bought it. Lianne and family members were supposed to receive the R700 000 back within 30 days once the unit was sold. It was sold for R1.4 Million in April 2020. But Lianne still has not seen a scent. She has opened both a criminal and civil case against the Belvedere Group and developer Billy E Steyn, who is in charge of the group. Gavin den Heyer: Has actually won a court case against the group, where the court ordered that Belvedere Group pay out the money owed to den Heyer in monthly instalments. Belvedere are still not paying. Lyn Cunningham: Her mother gave up her unit in Harveston to be sold, to pay for the costs of frail care she now needs. Although the un it was sold in 2019, Lyn and her mother have still not received any money.
metadata.Further information: Lianne Silver's lawyer, Reon Marais, has agreed to do an on camera interview. He is helping Lianne do the civil and criminal cases. Says that the group have no leg to stand on, contractually they have to pay. Even if their were a longer period involved, to get admin etc sorted, the group cannot not pay after months of already having the been paid for the properties. Also says Belvedere are not using any legal loopholes not to pay, they are simply not paying. Bill E Steyn is according to a source, returning from his holiday home in George tomorrow, Thursday 28 January. He seems near impossible to get hold of, no one has email address, phone nrs etc for him. The group have two offices, one inside one of the estates, and another which seems to be the address of a law firm in Honeydew. I will start with a written offer of an on camera right of reply to his attorney and and a sales agent if they won't give me his contact details. Should it be necessary to do a confront, we could try door stopping the offices.
